name: Fort Dearborn — powder magazine

documented_range.note: THE RANGE IS THE FORT'S, NOT THIS BUILDING'S. No source reached dates any individual building inside Fort Dearborn. It opens with the rebuild of 1816 and closes with the demolition of the fort's principal structures in the summer of 1856 (Andreas). What carries the scene date is the middle: the post was garrisoned continuously from June 1832 to 29 December 1836.

position.symbolic_location: Inside the south-west of Fort Dearborn, between the west end of the guard house and the block-house at the south-west angle.
position.note: PLACED BY A SENTENCE, NOT BY THE PLAN. The 1830 plan draws no magazine; the only positional evidence is Hubbard in 1827: 'the magazine, of brick, was situated about half way between the west end of the guard and block-houses.' That reading is what put the guard house on the WEST side of the south gate rather than the east - it is the only assignment of the two flanking buildings that leaves a real gap for the magazine to stand in - and this position is the midpoint of that gap, just inside the curtain in the south-west quarter of the enclosure. UNCERTAINTY IS LARGER THAN THE REST OF THE COMPLEX: 'about half way' is the whole of it, and the sentence can be parsed two ways (midway between the two buildings' west ends, or midway between the guard house's west end and the block-house), which move the point about 4 m apart. The rotation is the fort's.

derivation.reason: This placement predates the derivation module. Its provenance and reasoning are recorded in position.note, but no machine-checkable derivation block has been authored for it yet.

footprint.note: INVENTED. No source gives this building's size, and the 1830 plan does not draw it. 4.57 x 3.66 m is fifteen by twelve feet, which is a powder magazine for a two-company post and nothing more than that. The reason there is a polygon at all is that the alternative is not modelling a brick building two sources describe; the reason it is graded conjectural is that a visitor looking at this outline is looking at our arithmetic.

kind.note: Hubbard names it in 1827 and Andreas's summary of the rebuilt fort lists a magazine among what the stockade enclosed.

construction.note: Hubbard: 'the magazine, of brick'. One of only two brick buildings in the fort. GUARD ON A TEMPTING PARALLEL: the 1803 War Department instruction for this class of post specified 'the magazines for powder to be of brick of a conic figure', which is quoted in the same literature - but that is the specification for the FIRST fort, and it is not evidence that this magazine was conical. It is built as a plain gabled block.

stories.note: Not attested. A powder magazine is a single vaulted or single-storey room by definition of the type.

wall_height_m.note: Unattested. About eight feet of brick wall, which is what the type carries. A guess.

roof_type.note: Unattested. Gable rather than the conic figure of the 1803 specification, for the reason set out in the construction note - and either choice is ours.

roof_pitch_deg.note: No pitch is attested for any building in this fort. 34 degrees is the archetype's mid-range for a shingled or riven-shake roof of this period and span, inferred from construction practice rather than measured.

chimneys.note: A magazine has no chimney. That is not an absence of evidence; it is what the building type is for.

function.note: The garrison's powder store. Its brick construction is the one thing about it that is documented twice over - by its material and by the type - and its size, height and roof are all ours.

research_note: THE BUILDING WITH THE BEST-ATTESTED POSITION AND THE WORST-ATTESTED EVERYTHING ELSE. Hubbard's sentence locates it relative to two other buildings and no source gives it a dimension, a height or a roof; the 1830 plan, which draws everything else in this fort, does not draw it at all - either because it was too small for the plate or because it was gone by 1830, and nothing decides between those. It is built because two sources say a brick magazine stood in this fort and leaving it out would be the same kind of silence the exclusions file exists to prevent; it is graded conjectural throughout because everything a visitor can see about it is ours.

land_owner.value: The ground was entered by John Baptist Baubian, 28 May 1835
land_owner.note: THE UNITED STATES RESERVATION. This is the same tract L108 already derives for `1835_no_build_ground.json` — from G1, Madison's line and the traced waterline — so the polygon is inherited rather than built again, and `check.sh` already re-derives it. The register's own row is the second, independent witness to the date L108 quotes from Andreas: Beaubien's pre-emption, 28 May 1835, five weeks before the scene date. The derived polygon is short of the documented 75.69 acres for the reasons L108 states, and is a floor rather than the reservation. WHETHER THE ENTRY HELD IS NOT READ HERE: it was disputed, and this row records the entry the register carries and nothing about its outcome. THE MARGIN IS 51 m: this footprint stands that far inside the tract's nearest boundary, which is more than twice the working horizontal uncertainty of anything traced off the 1834 sheets (about 20 m), so the assignment survives the error the construction carries. WHAT THIS ROW CLAIMS AND WHAT IT DOES NOT. It claims that the tract the Illinois State Archives' land-sale register describes contains this structure's committed position — the patent for this ground was ENTERED by this man on this date. It does not claim he still held the ground on 1 July 1835, that he lived here, or that he ever stood on it: a sale is a transaction, and the register's only column about residence names a county. THE SECTION LINES ARE CONSTRUCTED, NOT TRACED (L219): the grid is carried from the single PLSS corner at State & Madison, on the plat's own east-west bearing, in nominal one-mile squares.
land_owner.tract: the south-west fractional quarter of section 10
